author: henry
sigSummary: From Camp McClellan, Henry tells his brother James of a drunken Confederate deserter who paddled a half-swamped boat across the Potomac to surrender to Henry's twelve-man picket post — cursing the sentries as "sons of biches" when they demanded the countersign, then refusing to go back when the rebels called him the next morning. Henry kept two rebel gun caps as souvenirs; Lt. Scott paid five dollars for the deserter's knife.
transcription:
Nov. 30, 1861
Camp McClellan

Dear James:

I was very glad to get a letter from you. I should like it if you would write often. I must tell you what news I can. When our company was on picket a secesh or reble came across the river, near our post. He came over as a deserter, had a very small boat. It was most full of water when he got over. He had a very fine gun and a large knife with him. We heard him paddling the water some time before he came across. There were twelve of us on post. We all had our guns loaded and our bayonets fixed for we did not know but what there was a large force of them. When he was nearly over we halted him and demanded the countersign, but he called us all sons of biches. He had been taking a drop before he came over. The rebles, next morning, wanted him to go back, but he would not. We can see the rebles quite plainly in the day time. They have fires all along the river at night. It is against the orders to talk with the rebles across the river.

I have got two secesh caps, those that they use for "Guns". Lt. Scott bought a large knife that the rebles brought over. He bought it for five dollars. He bought it for a curiosity to show when he goes home what the rebles use in war. No more this time.

I remain, your aff. Brother,

Henry.

author: henry
sigSummary: Writing from Camp McClellan, Henry sketches his brigade's order of battle: three New York regiments including the 2nd, the Minnesota regiment, and his own 34th NY, all drilling together two or three times a week under General Gorman. He has shaken off a bout of homesickness and gently corrects the rumors reaching home that his company has suffered — "It is not correct" — admitting only one hard stretch in Virginia.
transcription:
Nov. 30th, 1861
Camp McClellan

Dear Frances:

I was very glad to get a letter from you. I have been a little homesick lately, but I have got over it. I see you are forming plans for me when I go home. I hope they will turn out good. I should not wonder but they will, I hope so.

I saw Brink not long since, said he had received a letter from you, seemed to be in good humor. I have not continued my Journals. Have not had much time. Shall continue them next week. Our Company have all got new blankets, very heavy and good.

In regard to our Company suffering so mucy. It is not correct. There was one time in Virginia we had a pretty hard time, but that was all. We have a brigade drill two or three times a week, three Regts. of New York 2d and the Minnesota, besides ours. Gorman is General. I have nothing more to write at present. Write often.

I remain your aff. brother,

Henry

author: henry
sigSummary: Writing from Camp McClellan in cold so sharp he can scarcely hold his pen, Henry begs his worrying mother to "let your mind rest at perfect ease," reports he stands third or fourth in the furlough queue, and came off picket Thanksgiving day at two o'clock. He confesses he sometimes thinks he "did wrong to leave home" with the farm needing him that winter, yet pledges that "when I do get home I shall stay."
transcription:
Nov. 30, 1861

Dear Mother:

I received your letter last eve. It is so cold now that I can not write very good, but I shall do the best I can. I am sorry to know that you have been worrying about me. You must not. If I am sick I shall let you know, you must let your mind rest at perfect ease about me. I admit we suffer with the cold some, but that cannot be helped. Some of the boys have fireplaces in their tents and others have stoves. Have not any in our tent. The stoves cost between three and four dollars. When we go into winter quarters we shall probably have log houses, but we shall have to build them.

I received two papers from home, one was the Observer and the other, New York Times. Very glad to receive them. In regard to my having a furlough to go home. I do not think I can get one at present. There are three or four before me now. I understand that two can only go at one time. I should like to go home if I could. The war may be over before I go. I hope it may. I came off from picket Thanksgiving day at two o'clock in the afternoon.

I am, of course, perfectly willing to pay my portion in regard to the taxes, or anything else. Very glad to do so. I had my picture taken, but could not get it standing. It cost me a dollar, the case and all. You wrote about sending me some mittens, but if I had a pair of woolen gloves they would be very acceptable. I bought a pr. of buckskin, but they are not very warm.

I sometimes think that I did wrong to leave home, knowing that you will need me this winter, but when I do get home I shall stay. I think that you got along very well last summer in regard to farming. That is, I think the boys worked it very well although the crops did not turn out very well.

I have no more time to write now. More next time. Write often.

I remain your aff. Son,

Henry

author: alexander
sigSummary: Alexander's first army pay reaches Camp Jackson — and he sends fifteen of his seventeen dollars home, half-joking he'll have his Mother "courtmartialed" if she won't buy herself a warm winter cloak. He recounts a sentry's rifle going off on the picket bridge, taking off a man's thumb, and now cautions his own reliefs to carry their arms with care. He clings to the verse Frances wrote in his Bible — "God is our refuge and strength."

health.detail: Happy, independent, religious; "dependent on no one"
Right thumb shot off; will be discharged

transcription:
Dec. 8, 1861
Camp Jackson

My Dear Mother:

Don't you think I was glad to hear from home, eh? Why when I received those four letters I hardly knew whether I was on my head or feet. You wish me to acknowledge all the letters that I receive. I have received one mailed Nov. 18, another Nov. 6th. (I believe the figures are not very plain.) Another Dec. 3 and one from Henry mailed Dec. 4. I have not received any papers as yet. I never enjoyed anything more than the reading of those letters.

We received our pay last Friday morning up to the first of November. I received seventeen dollars and thirty-three cents. I have sent home fifteen dollars. The Capt. sends it for me. He sends it to George Dunning. Dunning will pay it over to you as soon as he received it. Now, my dear Mother, I give it all to you. This is the first time that I have been able to make my Mother a present and I want you to take it. If you do not I shall feel very, very bad. I want you to buy you a nice warm cloak for winter or else a warm woolen dress and a warm pair of gaiters. Now if you disobey my orders I shall feel very much like having you courtmartialed. It is rather a bad thing to fall into the hands of such a court. You had not better disobey. I give you fair warning.

Quite a sad accident happened night before last. (Luther and I were on guard duty). David Dava[?]way, one of the pickets on a bridge a little below the camp, while stepping off from a wall, in some way stumbled and dropt his rifle. He endeavored to catch the piece with his right hand, but before he could do so it struck against a stone and went off. The ball passed through his right thumb between the first and second joints and almost graised his head. His thumb was taken off. He will be discharged. When I go out with my reliefs, I am oblige to caution the men with "men be careful how you carry your rifles". They sometimes carry them very carelessly. Tell Frances I shall never forget the text she wrote in my bible, "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble." He is such indeed to me. Love to all.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander

Dec. 9 — We are now having very warm weather. The weather today promises to be quite sultry. I was really uncomfortable yesterday on account of the heat. Luther and I are on guard duty today. Send me papers as often as you can. We have nothing to read here. Tell Frances I will write her soon. I shall give you the direction again for fear that you will forget them. Direct to Baltimore, Md. Sixtieth Regt. N.Y. S. A. Co. H, care of Capt. Ransom.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander

P.S. You ask me in one of your letters "how I like soldiering" and to be candid xxxx about it, I like it very well. Mother, I am dependent on no one. That is a great comfort to me. I shall try and get a pass tomorrow to go to Baltimore and have my miniature taken.

author: alexander
sigSummary: Alexander writes from Camp Jackson, near Baltimore, having finally received four home letters in a bunch — "I feel about five hundred per cent better" — after a lost knapsack swallowed his earlier letter and writing materials. At Charley's request he sketches camp life minute by minute, from the half-past-five reveille to the day's rations of bread, beef, and green coffee. Then he turns urgent: James must never give up the idea of an education — "Never — never, never."
transcription:
Dec. 8, 1861
Camp Jackson

My dear Brother:

I have at length heard from home. Four letters all in a bunch. Doing pretty well — don't you think so? I feel about five hundred per cent better. You have no idea how much good they have done me. It took me nearly two hours to read them all. It seems to me that I never spent that space of time so pleasantly before.

So you thought I had forgotten you all at home. Well, well, well, I thought you knew me better than that, but then I don't wonder at it. It was no fault of mine that you did not hear from me sooner. You may be sure of that. I began a letter when we were at Kalarama Heights. When we arrived at Camp Jackson it was quite late in the evening. We were obliged to stack our arms and knapsacks prior to pitching our tents. I was detailed for guard duty that night, and Luther as one of an escort to the Major as he was oblige to go back to the Relay House on business — so that I had no one to look after my knapsack. A sergeant in Company C took it by mistake and I did not find it until quite a number of days afterward. The letter and my writing materials were in it. Now you see that I was not to blame.

Charley in his letter (how I should like to see him) asks me to "write all the minute details of my life" in Camp. I will do my best. Reveille beats at half-past five. As soon as I hear the drum (almost the first tap wakes me) I spring up, put my cap, jacket and shoes on (I generally sleep with them off) turn out and fall into line. We are allowed only five minutes to do all this in. At the expiration of the five minutes the Orderly proceeds to call the roll. If any are absent they are placed on guard duty with their knapsacks on. It is no small thing to carry a knapsack for seventy-four hours.

After roll call one of the men from our tent goes to the Commissaries and draws the ration for the tent. (one loaf of bread, one and a fourth pounds of beef or three fourths of a pound of pork or bacon per each man, and a certain amount of sugar and rice or hominy or potatoes and some tea. We also have coffee, but as it is green it is not served out to the company. We then set to work to get breakfast (except the Commissary (he tents with us) and those on guard duty.) Some get the water, another cooks the meat, another makes the tea, etc., etc., etc. We get along "first rate". At half past eight comes guard mounting. It would take up too much room to tell you how it is done. I will finish the synopsys of the day in another letter as I have not much more room.

I am very glad to hear that you are to attend Mr. Partridges convention. Improve your time. Learn all you can. Now James, don't you never give up the idea of getting an education. Never — never, never. Don't be discouraged. You CAN do it if you have health. Now you must not be vexed at me for saying what I have, a little fellow like me. I feel very anxious that you should do well. If my life is spared, when I return won't I put in, eh?

I understand from one of the letters that you could have had the position of Orderly Sergeant if you could have got five men. I was almost sorry at first that you did not accept of it, but on reflection I think you have done well. You now stand a chance of getting into West Point, whereas if you had enlisted that is forever done for besides to take three or even two years out of your life now, would make it useless to try to get an education. There I am talking like an old man, well, well, well, what next.

Your affectionate Brother,

Alex F. Hubbell

author: alexander
sigSummary: His furious sketch of a Baltimore swindle: Alexander tells Mother two "pictures" cost thirteen shillings, lamenting "that which is dearly bought is apt to be prized." The first portrait so enraged him he "felt like making a bayonet charge upon the one who took it," vowing a better likeness "if it costs me fifty dollars." The joint photograph with Luther he asks her to hide away and show no one — "a memorial of our soldiering together."
transcription:
Dec. 11th, 1861
Camp Jackson

My dear Mother:

Here is my "picture." Luther and I were at Baltimore yesterday and had them taken. I was badly cheated on account of my inexperience in such things. Those two "pictures" cost thirteen shillings. That which id dearly bought is apt to be prized. I shall profit by this experience. The picture in which Luther and I are taken cost ten shillings. When that picture was given to me I felt like making a bayonet charge upon the one who took it. I said to myself "I cannot and will not send home that picture. I will have another taken if it costs me fifty dollars." I went to another gallery and had the other taken which cost three shillings. If you think it is worth it you had better have it put in a case as it is easily spoilt. The other picture I want you to put safely away in some drawer and show it to no one. The only reason why I send it is I want to keep it as a memorial of our soldiering together.

My dear Mother, will you be so kind as to send me some postage stamps. I will refund the money to you next pay day. I feel bad to think I have spent so much money. I want to be very economical. I am enjoying excellent health. The weather has been very warm and pleasant. Love to all.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander.

author: alexander
sigSummary: Capt. Ransom climbs aboard a passing freight train during the "Grand Rounds" near Camp Jackson — and survives a boiler explosion that kills everyone else on the engine. Alexander gives his sister Frances a harrowing, almost forensic account: the engineer hurled hundreds of feet through a tree, the iron dome flung thirty rods, the fireman left burning in a ditch until Ransom puts out the flames with his bare hands. Not even a scratch on him.

health.detail: Was sick recently; Ransom brought toast and tea; now well enough for guard duty

transcription:
Dec. 16, 1861
Camp Jackson

My dear Sister:

I wonder what sort of weather you are having up there. Pretty cold I guess, eh? The weather here is warm and sunshiney — very much like our September weather.

We came very near losing our Captain the other night but then "an inch of a miss", you know, "is as good as a mile." I feel very, very thankful that his life was spared to the Company. I hardly think his place could have been filled. The Major paid him quite a compliment the other day. He said to the Company "You have a good Capt." and that was a great deal for him.

Now I suppose you would like to hear how Capt. Ransom came so near losing his life. It was about as narrow an escape as I ever heard of. The only marvel is that he is now living. I can almost hear you say, "Out with it you provoking boy." Well, "here goes". The Capt. was going the "Grand Rounds". One of the officers is obliged to go over the line every night between the hours of one and six to see that the sentries are awake on their posts doing their duty and are properly instructed. This is called the "Grand Rounds". A freight train just then passed and as it was going slow he jumped on to ride out to one of the pickets about a quarter of a mile distant. (The freight engines on this road are different from those up North. They are fed with coal. The cabin is directly over the boiler which extends back so that the fireman standing upon a platform of the tender (which is open in front) is able to shovel coal into it. The Capt. stood upon the platform with the fireman. He (the fireman) had just commenced "firing up" when the boiler burst blowing the engineer, I presume, two or three hundred feet into the air. In his descent he fell through a tree breaking a limb about three inches in thickness, and on xxxx striking the ground he bounded and fell some fifteen or twenty feet from where he first struck. The Capt. stood still for a moment "thunder struck" I suppose when it occurred to him that the cars might come pileing one upon another, as they had been under some headway. He stepped off and started to go up the bank (about twenty feet in heighth.) When about half way up the body of a soldier (Haine, I believe) fell close beside him and pieces of the wreck all around him. If some of those large pieces had struck him they would have killed him instantly. The dome (weighing I should judge a ton perhaps, two, three or four) was thrown some thirty rods from the engine. The engineer was thrown about twenty-five rods. You can have some idea how high the men were thrown from the time it took them to fall.

The Capt. soon heard some one calling for help and immediately went in search of him. He found the fireman on fire and extinguished the fire by throwing water upon him from the ditch with his hands. The fireman died a day or two after. The Capt. is the only one that escaped alive of those upon the engine. He did not receive even a scratch. The fireman was so badly burned that he died, and Capt. Ransom standing beside him not even scratched. We certainly have great reason to be thankful.

Now, Miss Fannie, I want you to write me often — very often — once a week certainly. You tell James and Charles if they don't write me more often I will pull their ears for them when I get home. I certainly shall and they may look out for their noses, too. I have received four papers and letter dated Dec. 9 since I last wrote. You would never neglect writing me if you knew how much good that letter did me. Do not forget to send me some postage stamps to frank our letters. The ladies of Chazy are making up a box to send to those in the Company who came from there. I wish the ladies of Champlain would follow their example. Some warm woolen gloves would be very acceptable indeed.

Mr. Luther wrote Amos for a list of the names of those who came from Chaney. I do not have many idle moments. I am on guard duty tomorrow if all is well. I was up to Baltimore yesterday to church. I will tell you about it in another letter. I have sent my "picture" home. I will let you and Mother settle which shall have it. Capt. Ransom was very, very, very, very kind to me when I was sick. He came often to see me and brought me toast and tea a number of times. I wish Mother would write him a note. It would please him. Love to all.

Your affectionate brother,

Alexander.

P.S. I see by the papers that there is danger of war with England. Let her come, I am as ready to fight Britons as Southerners. If she does interfere I hope my brothers and every other able bodied man will turn out and help us fight. I hope our regiment will be sent up the frontier.

author: henry
sigSummary: From Camp McClellan, two days before Christmas, Henry expects the 34th New York to settle into winter quarters guarding the Potomac — the Minnesota regiments are raising log houses and his own regiment is building a hospital, signs enough that "this looks somewhat like staying." He watches discipline tighten: the old sutler drummed out for selling liquor, gamblers made to stand on a barrel six hours without food. Still unable to reach his brother Alexander, he confesses he gets very lonesome now and then.
transcription:
Dec. 19th, 1861
Camp McClellan

Dear Chas:

I received a letter from you and also two papers. We are having very fine weather for this time of the year. Our Co. came off from picket yesterday. The probability is now that our Regt. will stay here for winter quarters to guard the Potomac. That is what I heard. The Minnesota Regts. are fixing up for winter, building log houses. Our Regt. is also building a hospital. This looks somewhat like staying.

You wished to know who tents with me. They ar strangers to me. E. Graves from Chasy and John Green and A. Perkins. Pleasant fellows, but I would rather tent with some of the Champlain boys, but the tents are all full. I get very lonesome now and then. I go on line guard every week. We have three drills every day besides dress parade. We have also three Brigade drills every week. Three Regts. besides our march in line of battle, etc., etc. The old sutler was drumed out of Camp yesterday for selling licor, good for him, but some of the boys don't like it. We have one sutler in our Camp now. I have not got any tickets from him since pay day nor do I intend to. He charges to much. The boys cannot get anything to drink but cider now.

I am much oblige to you for sending me some of my money. I am not shure that I will get a pr. of boots. If I do not I think I will not use the money. In regard to sending money home — I paid 31 cts. freight. After this I shall send home my money in a letter. It is about as safe. I have not heard from Alexander yet. I have written him, but it seems that the direction is not correct. I shall write him soon. So far as I know the boys from Champlain like soldiering very well. Col. L--- has resigned so I have heard. Good many of the boys thought he was a coward. He has a very good voice. xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx A good many of the boys pass away there time by playing cards, but I have not learned yet. If they are caught at it they are severely punished. Some of our Regt. were caught gambling the other night. They will have to stand on a barrel six hours without any food and four dollars taken off their wages. Write often. I am your aff. Brother,

Henry

author: henry
sigSummary: Writing from Camp McClellan, three miles from Poolesville, Henry reports eight rebels crossing the lines as deserters with word that the enemy "have nothing to eat" — a soldier's-eye glimpse of Confederate hunger on the Potomac. With little else to tell in the sameness of winter quarters, he confesses the cold has stopped his journal, a thing he'll be sorry for if he gets home, and admits he'd give much to be back for the village sing school.
transcription:
Dec. 20th, 1861
Camp McClellan

Dear Frances:

I send this letter by B. Miner. He starts tomorrow morning for Champlain. I gave him my other letter also. The reason why I did not write to you before is because I had nothing to write about. Everything goes on here about the same from day to day. I have got an accordian. Bill Robers offered to learn me how to play on it. I have not made much progress yet, but I will after a while. You know how I play the violin. I have not continued my journal any since it has been so cold. That is one thing I shall be sorry for if I ever get home. I heard through one of the boys from Champlain that they had a sing school there, I should like to attend if I was at home. Albert has been home and had a fine time sleigh riding as I heard. To day eight rebels came across to our side as deserters. They say the rebels have nothing to eat. We went to church today — Capt. Rich preached. Poolesville is about three miles from our camp. Write often.

I am your aff. Brother,

Henry

author: henry
sigSummary: From winter quarters at Camp McClellan, Henry writes home with a soldier's pride: at brigade drill, Gen. Gorman told the regiment "they did the best of them all" — "we felt quite proud, I tell you." Yet he still cannot reach his brother Alexander, having written to Washington on a direction now proving wrong: "It seems bad that we cannot correspond." Unsettled by the swearing and gambling around him, Henry insists a man keeps good morals in camp only if "very strict and firm."
transcription:
Dec. 20th, 1861
Camp McClellan

Dear Mother:

We have had a Brigade drill today. Gen. Gorman told our Regiment that they did the best of them all. We felt quite proud, I tell you. I have found a dictionary here. Some of the boys bought one in Washington. I think I shall buy one and send home. It is a very good one. I have written to Alex, but directed to Washington, that was the direction he gave me. I have not heard from him. We hear that Washington is the wrong direction. I do not know his Regt. I shall write again soon. It seems bad that we cannot correspond. A man cannot live in Camp and maintain good morals unless he is very strict and firm. There is so much swearing and gambling that it is enough to ruin any young man. Four men in our company were caught playing cards the other night. They will have to stand on a barrel six hours and two or four dollars taken from their wages. A man in the Minnesota Regt. shot himself through the arm the other day accidentally. How it was done I have not learned. I am well and hope this will find you the same. Write often.

I am your aff. son,

Henry

author: alexander
sigSummary: Company H, singled out as one of the best in the regiment, is pulled by Colonel Hayward into Baltimore to replace Company C guarding Camden Station, the Baltimore & Ohio depot. Alexander writes from a three-story brick building where five tentmates sing and brew tea on the Captain's stove. Promoted from seventh to fourth Corporal in three months, he still grumbles, playfully: a soldier who writes twice to their once, and feels neglected.
transcription:
Dec. 22, 1861
Baltimore

My dear Brother:

You perceive by the heading of my letter that we have moved camp. Colonel Hayward being dissatisfied with the conduct of Company C and as Company H had the reputation of being the best, or at least one of the best "companies" in the Regt. he ordered us to take their place. We are quartered in a three story brick building on the outskirts of the City and are guarding a branch railway about three miles in length running from the main road (Baltimore and Ohio) to another end of the city. The depot is called the Camden Station. Luther and I have a first rate room. Five others "tent" with us. One of us are singing — others writing. We make music. It is almost time to get supper. Now I suppose you would like to know how we will go to work to "get it". Well, in the first place we fill our "mess pan" with water. In the next place we put it on the stove (we have the Captains), in the third we put some tea or coffe in it and let it boil, and in the fourth place we put in some sugar and drink it. We sometimes cook beef or port. One of our men says he will get some cabbage tonight for soup tomorrow.

Now, Master James, you must excuse this wandering, disconnected letter. We have been singing and sometimes when I was in the midst of a sentence I would "pitch in". You know that two things can not be done at once and be done well. Don't you think my excuse good — eh? I have been holding an indignation meeting with myself. Why don't you all write me more often. I — a solider — with barely any conveniences write twice to your once. Now — I feel really neglected — yes, neglected. Ask Mother and Frances and Charles and yourself if you have forgotten me. I received two papers yesterday. Don't forget to send some postage stamps. I have risen three grades. When I left the North I was seventh Corporal. I am now fourth. Luther has also risen three grades. He was eighth and is now fifth. Love to all.

Your affectionate Brother,

Alexander

P.S. Has Mother received that fifteen dollars I sent her and my miniature?

author: alexander
sigSummary: Preston King is in Baltimore, Alexander reports, "trying to have the Regiment sent North to guard the frontiers" — and so, the corporal hints, he may be home sooner than expected. Yet his Christmas turns wistful: "I a soldier hundreds of miles from home! How funny, eh?" He delights that the white cow has a new "bossy," marches seven men out to relieve the pickets, and adds that Mason and "Stidell" have reportedly been released.
transcription:
Dec. 23, 1861
Baltimore

My Dear Mother:

I have received a letter from you today and very glad I was to hear that you are all so well. Your letter contains some strange news — very strange. Champlain again to be occupied by United States troops — well — well — well. What next? "Stranger things have happened." I will not tell you something about as strange. I may be home a little sooner than you expected. Preston King is here it is said trying to have the Regiment sent North to guard the frontiers.

Dec. 25. Christmas is it? So it is. I a soldier hundreds of miles from home! How funny, eh? Luther and I were out in the City yesterday. Baltimore is quite a city. There is no lack of "darkies" here. I wonder what you are doing up there today! How I should like to be with you all today, but then there is no use in wishing. It cannot be. I feel rather lonely today. You have no idea how much good your letters did me. I was particularly pleased to hear that the "white cow" had a little "bossy". I should indeed like to be at home to enjoy the "new milk cow". I should like to return and see you all, nevertheless I am very well contented where I am.

Dec. 23, 1861 — Contd.

You tell James that I do not doubt his good intentions, but if he waits until vacation to write I am afraid that letter never will be forthcoming.

Dec. 26. Luther, Orderly Dickinson, I and three others were out in the city. We went into an eating saloon and got dinner. It cost me a quarter. I find the only place to get a Christmas dinner is at home. I also find that it does not pay to get dinner in these eating saloons. I am on guard duty today. At one oclock I have a relief of seven men to take out to relieve the pickets along the line (about two miles.) Now you have some idea of the duties of a Corporal.

Love to all. Give my respects to Mr. Copeland. I have written grandmother McNiel.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander.

P.S. It is reported that Mason and Stidell have been released.

author: henry
sigSummary: Writing from Camp McClellan, Henry tells his mother he has at last heard from his brother Alexander — the letter found him despite a direction "not quite correct" — and relays Alex's word that Capt. Ransom "had a narrow escape." Between buying a $3.50 sheet-iron stove against the cold and a promise to send $25 home next pay day, Henry sheepishly vows to mind his spelling, "writing in a hurry" to a mother he knows reads every line.
transcription:
Dec. 26, 1861
Camp McClellan

Dear Mother:

I received a letter from you Christmas Eve. Glad to know that you are all well. We are having cold weather, but no snow. Our Co. came off from picket this morning, was on for twenty-four hours. Went on Christmas morning.

Dec. 27th. Today is quite warm from what it has been. I have bought a stove for our tent. It cost $3.50. I advanced the money. It was so cold that I could not get along without it. The stove is made of sheet iron. There will be twenty-one shillings coming to me for the stove next pay day. It cost seven shillings apiece for four of us. I shall try to send home next pay day $25.00. We get paid off by the 15th of Jan. We are having barracks built for our Regt. There are so many men detailed for making them, but I have not been yet. They get extra pay for it. The soldiers do all the wood cutting. The teamsters draw it. It takes a great quantity to supply the Regt.

We have the same Chaplain now that we had at first. Have a prayer meeting every Sunday evening, but I have not been yet, for it so happened, that most every Sabbath I have been on guard. There is not much of any Sabbath here.

I find our stove very comfortable. You need have no fear but what I shall get my money back. I have received a letter from Alex. He seems to like soldiering very well. He has received that letter I wrote him although the direction was not quite correct. He wrote that Capt. Ransom had a narrow escape. I suppose he has written you all about it. I have not much of news to write you. You get it up North faster than we do. I hope Silas will get that accordian. I shall be very careful of it.

I have nothing more to write. I shall be more careful after this and not have so much bad spelling. Sometimes I have to write in a hurry and do not take so much pains as I might or as I should. We have in our Camp a man who takes pictures. He has got the whole rigging.

I do my own washing every week and try to keep myself as clean as I can. Most all the soldiers do their washing. Last summer I washed in cold water, but now I have it warmed.

I remain your aff. Son,

Henry

author: alexander
sigSummary: At Camp Jackson the sentinel's challenge ran word for word — "Number ### — Advance" — and after three unheeded halts at night, each guard fired his piece to alarm the camp. Writing from Baltimore, Alexander sets down a corporal's day with an ethnographer's care: two-hour relief rotations, a king's-worthy kettle of beef, pared potatoes and cabbage, his own long vigils by the fire. On New Year's morning he pictures James reading the January Harper's at home.
transcription:
Dec. 29, 1861
Baltimore

My dear Brother:

You tell Frances that I shall not write her again until she writes me. That I am really provoked with her. I have received two letters from home within a few days and not a word or message did she write or send. You are nearly — yes — just as bad. Now do you both "mend your ways". I shall have you both "hauled up" before a "Court of Inquiry" if you dont look out.

I began a "Synopsis of a day in Camp" in a letter to James. I shall now try and finish it in this. I believe I left off at "Guard Mounting". That interesting ceremony sometimes comes off (always at half past eight, before some of the men have finished or even began breakfast. If they are on the "first relief" they are immediately marched off to their posts and are obliged to stand there until eleven. You see this has a tendency to make the men prompt and smart "right up the handle" as the soldiers say. (Whenever this is the case the men usually before going out catch up a piece of bread and run).

I shall try and get a pass and attend service this evening. I have attended once today.

Dec. 30. I attended service again last evening. It seemed like old times. I enjoyed the singing very much. This love of singing seems to be a perfect passion with the soldiers. The church has a very fine organ. I am wandering from my story.

If I am on guard duty I am obliged to take out a part of the relief guard in one direction and the other Corporal in another and the Sergeant places the remainder around the Camp. (I am now speaking as though I were at Camp Jackson.) (I presume you would like to know what orders the sentinels have.) When within six paces of a sentinel I halt the "relief" and command "Number ### — Advance". He advances up to the sentinel and both stand at "arms apart". The sentinel then proceeds to give his orders "I am ordered to guard this road from — to —, to let no one meddle in anyway with the track or wires except those working on the road, and keep a sharp lookout on them. Halt every soldier that comes along and demand a pass. If he has none, take him prisoner and hand him over to the next sentinel. (Thus you see that he could be passed down to Camp without the sentinel leaving his post. "Arrest any person that you may think suspicious. You need not (a sentinel is now "calling" Corporal of the No. 1) stop commissioned officers". The relieved sentinel then falls in the rear and the relief proceeds. The night is the hardest part of the guard duty. At night the orders to the sentinels are the same as in the day time with the exception that they halt every one the comes along when within gun shot. If any one does not stop after being halted three times by the sentinel, he is fired upon. Each sentinel in succession discharges his piece and thus the Camp is alarmed. The Guard is immediately drawn up at a distance from the fire and a reconnoitering party is then sent out to ascertain what is the matter.

As I have said above, the night is the hardest part of it. All the shelter we have is a small tent capable of holding four or five men. The remainder of the Guard "camped down" around the fire. I generally sat up by the fire all night. Sometimes I would take my blanket and stretch out on the ground. Many a night when you have been sleeping comfortably in your bed have I been keeping my vigils by the guard fire. Every two hours the relief is called out. I take my men go out and relieve the sentinel, return and sit by the fire until the next two hours and thus it continues through the night.

At nine A.M the old Guard is marched out to discharge their guns. We sometimes fire in a volley, sometimes by file, and sometimes at a target. Those not on guard cook for those on.

(I will now take a day when I am not on guard and try and give you an account of how I spend my time. I have already in a former letter described how the morning is passed. I believe I omitted one thing. Before (sometimes not till after) breakfast I take a towel and soap and go down to the brook which runs through our Camp and have a "good wash". It is really refreshing. I feel like taking half-a-dozen "somersets" after it. After breakfast I usually take out my rifle (these tents are a great place to rest them) clean and oil it up nicely. If I did not do this it would soon get so rusty that there would be no doing anything with it.

I will now suppose that beef was served out in our days rations and that we had cut all the meat off down to the bone and cooked it for breakfast. I now take a "camp kettle". Fill it two thirds full of water, hang it over the fire, put in the beef, potatoes (pared) and cabbage (if I can get it) and let it boil about an hour. I then season it with salt and pepper if it is to be had. That is soup fit for a king to eat. At least you would think so from the way we all pitched into it. For supper we usually make some tea and sometimes cook a little hominy or rice. Sometimes Luther and I would get a pass and go up town. Sometimes I would stretch out in my tent and go to sleep (after I had been all night and the previous day on guard duty.

At 4 P.M. all not on guard duty are obliged to go out and drill. If any are absent they are placed on guard duty next day with a knapsack of twenty-five, thirty and thirty-five pounds weight. As I have said before I do not have many idle moments. I hate a lazy man. I have quite a number of letters generally to write. It is now late and I have no more time to write. You must excuse this disconnected letter.

Well, my man, you have just saved yourself from the clutches of the law. I have received a letter from you today. So Frances is really going to Canada. I am glad for her sake and sorry for Mothers. How pleasant it must be at home this winter. As quiet up there as though there were no war. Cars are passing here continually loaded with cannon gun carriages, hay, flour, pork, beef, etc, etc, etc. Large numbers of troops pass almost every day though not so large as when we first came on the road. We are, I understand, to be mustered in for pay tomorrow. We are to be inspected I believe at the same time by the Inspector General. New clothes will soon be given us.

Your affectionate brother,

Alexander.

P.S. I have received three letters from home within the last few days and one from Jerseyville. I have also received two papers, one Evangelist and one New York Times. Love to al and especially to Mother.

Dec. 31, 1861. 6½ A.M. You mention in your letter that on going home you "found James reading the January Harper and Mother and Frances talking". How pleasant and cozy that must have been. How I should like to be at home one of these long winter evenings. Wouldn't I have a jolly time, eh? In case of Englands interference I hardly ever expect to see home. I shall never lay down my arms until peace is restored. I hope you and James will show your "pluck" by joining the army, if there be a necessity. I have no more time.

Alexander

author: alexander
sigSummary: Alexander writes from Baltimore on New Year's Day, 1862, exhausted from a night's guard duty as the city's revelers "made quite a racket" — but proud to report his warrant as a non-commissioned officer, a corporal's equivalent of an officer's commission. He quotes its grand opening verbatim: "Know Ye That reposing special trust and confidence... in Alexander F. Hubbell." Tired and "really ashamed" of the brief note, he still thanks the family for the welcome postage stamps.
transcription:
January 1st, 1862
Baltimore

A happy New Year to you all:

The holidays are great days down here. The Baltimoreans made quite a racket last night. I was on guard duty and heard it all. I just write this to let you know that I am in the land of the living. I am enjoying excellent health and spirits. I received my warrant today. Each non-commissioned is obliged to have one of these. It is the same to them as a commissioned officers Commission. Mine runs in this wise "Know Ye That reposing special trust and confidence in the patriotism, valor, fidelity and abilities of Alexander F. Hubbell I do hereby appoint him, etc."

I Have received all the letters and papers you have sent me I think. Those postage stamps were especially welcome. Now you must excuse this note. I feel really ashamed of it.

I again wish you a happy New Year. I do not feel very bright after my yesterdays guard duty. Ask Mr. Copeland to write me. I feel almost afraid to write him first. I promise I will answer promptly. I should like to hear from my Minister very much. Please excuse this.

Yours affectionately,

Alexander

author: henry
sigSummary: Writing from Camp McClellan after a New Year's of beer "from the Capt." and a few boys gone too drunk, Henry tells his mother his company has presented Capt. Reich a $125 sword — he gave a dollar on a private's pay, "some gave more and some less." The Minnesota band played most all night before the Colonel's tent. He longs for a furlough, but only married men may go, so he waits — lonesome for letters and the box of socks still stuck in Washington.
transcription:
January 9th, 1862
Camp McClellan

Dear Mother:

I was very glad to get a letter from you. Glad to know that you are all well. If you are sick I want you should write and let me know. Brink said he had a very pleasant visit in Champlain, only his visit was not long enough. I should like to get a furlough and make a visit home, but I do not think I could, for I understand that only the married men can go at present. I shall have to make up my mind to wait another time.

We are having very pleasant weather now. We had some snow, but it is all off. New Years was quite a merry time with some of the boys. We all received a good glass of beer from the Capt. Some of the boys got drunk, or drank a little more than was necessary. Our Company has presented Capt. Reich with a very nice sword. I gave a dollar towards it. Some gave more and some less. The sword cost $125. It is a very handsome sword.

The Minnesota band played most all night New Years. They came over into our Camp and played some very good tunes before the Colonel's tent. The box of socks has not arrived yet. I expect the box is in Washington.

I have nothing more to write at present. Write often. I get very lonesome if I do not get a paper or something else to read. Excuse this writing.

I remain your aff. Son,

Henry

P.S. Capt. Reich brother is in as sutler for this Regt.

author: henry
sigSummary: From Camp McClellan, Henry adds a few lines to his sister Frances and admits he has burned every letter he received from home: they took up too much room in his knapsack, and he did not want them on him "if I should go over into Virginia." Then his postscript turns the request around — "Please burn all my letters." He closes glad, for her sake, that she is going to teach in Montreal this winter — a quiet aside beside a plea that, obeyed, would have erased this entire correspondence.
transcription:
Jan. 9th, 1862
Camp McClellan

Dear Frances:

As I was writing to Mother I though I would add a few lines to you. Jan. 10th: It is very warm and pleasant today and very (??). It can not last long. I burnt all the letters that I received from home. They took up to much room in my knap-sack. Besides if I should go over into Virginia I should not want all of those letters with me. I received a letter from Nellie and Aunt Laura. I am glad for your sake that you are going to teach in Montreal this winter.

Please excuse this writing and all mistakes. I have forgot all about the Journal. I do not think I can make it very interesting. I hope to write another and a longer letter next time.

I remain your aff. Brother,

Henry

P.S. Please burn all my letters.

author: alexander
sigSummary: Alexander writes home from Baltimore, frantic that no letter has come since December 20 — "Are you all sick or are you dead?" Then the harder news: a picket from his own Company was killed on the ninth, and he helped bring in the body, "a sight that but few of our Company could bear." He quotes Henry's New Year letter — "who knows whether at the end of 1862 we will all be in the land of the living" — glad his brother "had not forgotten his God."
transcription:
Jan. 13, 1862
Baltimore

My Dear Mother:

The mail has arrived and no letter. What is the matter? The last letter I received from you is dated "Dec. 20". I received one from Charles dated "Dec. 22". That is the last I have received from home. What can be the reason? Are you all sick or are you dead? Something must be the matter for I know you would not forget me. What can be the matter? I am afraid you are sick. Do not keep me in suspense any longer. Let some one of the family write. Why don't Frances write and James, and Charles. Well — well — it certainly is strange. I have a great deal of news to write, but "shant" write a word until I hear from home.

One of our pickets (from our Company) was killed on the ninth of this month. I went out and helped to bring him in and saw a sight that but few of our Company could bear (I have my courage "screwed up" to almost anything). Now, my dear mother, if you want me to describe the affair, funeral and all, you must write me. (I hope to get a letter in this way). I have my letters filed, and they will show whether my friends are faithful in writing or not. I received a letter from Henry mailed on the sixth and was very glad to hear from him. He says, speaking of the New Year "who knows whether at the end of 1862 we will all be in the land of the living. It matters not when we leave this world if we are only right in the sight of God." I was very glad to have him say this for it showed me he had not forgotten his God, as most in the camp seem to have done.

I have not much spirit to write. Please write soon. Love to all.

Your affectionate son,

Alexander

author: alexander
sigSummary: Lonely at Camden Station, Baltimore, Alexander hasn't heard from home since December 22 and conjures Champlain swept off by the Chazy River or buried in snow until "the Sixtieth" digs them out. Ordered to replace the ailing Corporal Myers, he writes now from "head quarters" in the first platoon, wonders whether to buy a revolver for hauling off armed drunken soldiers, and signs himself "Corporal A. F. Hubbell" — a precious Bible his one comfort.
transcription:
Jan. 15, 1862
Camden Station
Baltimore

My Dear Mother:

You have no idea how lonely I am. I have not heard from home since the twenty-second of Dec. I am imagining almost everything. Are you all sick or are you dead. Perhaps the Chay River has overflowed its banks and swept Champlain into oblivion. It may be that the earth has opened and swallowed it up. But I think the most probable thing is that you are completely buried up in the snow. If that is the case you (if such a thing be possible) had better send us a message and "the Sixtieth" will come and dig you out. But what is the use of my talking in this way. I feel very — very anxious about you all. I hope you do not suffer for want of money. I hope you will not scruple to use my money. Every cent is yours. I shall soon receive my pay (twenty six dollars.) You perceive by the heading of my letter that I have again changed my quarters. Corporal Myers was taken sick and I was ordered to take his place. So that I am now in the first platoon or in other words "at head quarters". We take our meals at the "Union Relief."

I will tell oh! so much, if you will only write. What do you think about my getting a revolver. What do you think about my getting a revolver. There is a great demand for "Corporal of the Guard with a file of men" to take drunken soldiers to the guard or station house. These soldiers often carry knives or pistols. Perhaps my bayonet will be enough. You can see what it is in my "picture."

Will you be so kind as to send me some postage stamps. I am out. I shall try and get one from the Capt. to send this letter. Perhaps the reason you do not write is that you are so busy getting Frances off that you have not time to write. My greatest fear is that you are sick. Take good care of yourself. I have no notion of coming home and not finding you there. I have got a "precious Bible" from the Clinton County Bible Society. It is a great comfort to me.

Please write soon and do not forget the stamps.

Your affectionate son,

Corporal A. F. Hubbell

author: alexander
sigSummary: Porter has been killed upon the track. Roused from a mattress at a sick mess-mate's side, Alexander joined the squad that found him three-quarters of a mile out, "literally cut in two." Writing from Camden Station, Baltimore, he records the inquest and the funeral with a soldier's exactness — corporal and eight men, arms reversed, three volleys over the vault — then turns, stung, to defend why he enlisted: not "for the novelty," but to fight for his native land.
transcription:
Jan 17, 1862.
Camden Station — Baltimore

My Dear Brother:

I received a letter from home yesterday and no one who has not been from home can imagine how glad I was to hear from there. I thought you had all forgotten me. So Frances has really gone. You must be very lonely there this winter. How I envy your long quiet pleasant evenings. What are you studying at school this winter? How do Mr. and Mrs. Dobbin get along. Any more "hair pulls" yet, eh? So Dobbin did not want his wife to eat "nasty orange peel picked off from the floor", eh? How I wish I had been there. I should have had a regular ha ha. I suppose old Dobbin would have taken my head off. How I should like to see him and Mrs. D. get into a "squabble". I should enjoy it up to ninety-nine. What am I talking about. Write me all about home matters. I feel much more interested in matters concerning the "pig", old white cow and calf, and the pony than in anything else.

Have you drawn any more beach logs this winter. Rather unprofitable business with that little "pony" I think. How has Plummer fulfilled his contract? I am afraid you will get shaved. Keep a sharp lookout on him. He will lookout for No. 1, never fear.

(Contd.)

Jan. 17, 1862 — (Contd.

Now I suppose you would like to hear about that "sad accident" that happened here some days since. I had just thrown myself down on a mattress to "snoose" a few moments (I was helping to take care of a sick mess mate) when Sergeant Finch came to the door of the Lieutenants room and roared out Lieutenant, Lieutenant, Porter has been killed upon the track. Shall I take some men and bring him in? I immediately jumped up, put on my overcoat, went down and joined the squad. We had gone about three quarters of a mile when we came upon the body. It was a heart rending sight. He lay partly under the cars and was I might say, literally cut in two as the body only hung together by the cords and muscles of the back. A large piece of his back bone was torn out and lay some distance away. A large piece of flesh lay all around. His liver and entrails were also torn out and pieces of flesh lay all around.

Jan. 21 — I will finish this narrative in another letter. I am enjoying excellent health though I have had a severe cough and cold and am not entirely over them yet. I try to obey your injunctions "to take care of my health". When I read in your letter what Brink Miner said I felt just mad enough to kick him. (Excuse me for saying it.) I wonder if he thinks every one is like him, not two seconds content in one place. I did not enlist only for the novelty of the thing as he did, but to try and take care of myself and to fight for my native land. I don't like to see a young man able to care for himself sit at home with his hands in his lap, or when he is employed to grumble, growl and fret about it, and wish himself out of it. I believe in making the best of everything. (at least I try to.) A man is a great deal happier for doing so.

I have changed my mind and think I will finish my "narrative" in this letter. It was as I have said before — a heartrending sight. The dim lantern light made it doubly so. We made a litter of boards and brought him down to camp. It was pretty tough work, as he was a very large man. We were obliged to be very careful when we lifted him on the litter he was so crushed. His body was completely crushed from the breast down, also his left arm and right leg. There was an ugly gash on his left temple. As soon as we arrived at the camp the Capt. was sent for. A room was immediately prepared and the Capt. laid him out as well as it could be done. An inquest was held next day and a verdict returned of accidental death by being run over by the cars. He was buried the day after the inquest.

Perhaps you would like to hear something about the funeral. First went a Corporal and eight men with arms reversed, next the Chaplain, next the hearse, and last the Company. The band for some reason was no there. When we arrived at the cemetery the coffin was placed in a vault and three volleys fired over it.

Good night. It is now late. Luther is snoring away like a good fellow. Write soon. Love to all. I will write about the Union Relief Association in another letter.

Your affectionate Brother,

Alexander

To James Hubbell esq.
